chapter_title: Programmatic Interaction with Polkadot-JS API: Setup and Queries

screens.title: Programmatic Interaction with Polkadot-JS API
screens.subtitle: Setup, connect, and query a Substrate-based chain from Node.js

narration.text: In this lesson you'll learn how to go beyond the browser UI and interact with a Substrate chain programmatically. We'll set up a small Node. js project, install the core Polkadot-JS A P I package, and write scripts that connect to a running node, inspect runtime information, and query on-chain state. This matters because production dApps and backend services cannot rely on manual clicks; they need reliable, scriptable access to chain data. You will see how the WsProvider establishes a WebSocket link to a node, how ApiPromise creates an asynchronous A P I instance, and how the api object is organized into query, rpc, consts, and more. A short example will show connecting to a local dev node and printing the chain name and node version. We'll also cover common pitfalls you will encounter: forgetting to await the A P I creation, providing an incorrect WebSocket URL, and mishandling Option types when reading storage. By the end of this chapter you'll be able to scaffold a project, run a connection script, perform typical queries like balances and constants, and interpret the Codec types the A P I returns. Keep the local node running and let's turn those manual checks into repeatable scripts.

keyIdea.title: Why programmatic access matters
keyIdea.text: Scripts and dApps use the Polkadot-JS API to automate queries, build UIs, and send transactions. The API exposes organized objects for queries, RPCs, constants, and transactions.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.2 › Intro

Programmatic Interaction with Polkadot-JS API

Interactive 16:9 Masterclass — terminal-first orientation to setup and queries

This chapter teaches how to scaffold a Node.js project, install @polkadot/api, create a WsProvider and ApiPromise connection, and run queries that read chain state and metadata. Practical examples and pitfalls are included.

In this lesson
Code walk-throughs
Queries & types
Setup
Create a Node.js project and install @polkadot/api. This provides the core classes you'll use.
Connect
Use WsProvider and ApiPromise.create to open a WebSocket connection to your node and await readiness.
Query
Use api.query, api.rpc, and api.consts to read on-chain state, node properties, and runtime constants.
Quick demo
Connect and print chain details
const { ApiPromise, WsProvider } = require('@polkadot/api');

async function main () {
  const provider = new WsProvider('ws://127.0.0.1:9944');
  const api = await ApiPromise.create({ provider });
  console.log(`Connected to chain: ${api.genesisHash.toHex()}`);
  await api.disconnect();
}

main().catch(console.error);
Why this matters
Automated access to chain state lets backends and UIs fetch latest balances, block numbers, and custom pallet data without manual inspection.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.subtitle: Set up, connect, query, and interpret Polkadot-JS API results

narration.text: These objectives focus your work so you can build reliable scripts against a Substrate chain. First, you'll scaffold a Node. js project and install the core package, which lets your code import the WsProvider and ApiPromise classes. Second, you'll initialize the Polkadot-JS A P I correctly and understand the need to await ApiPromise. create so the connection lifecycle is handled. Third, you'll programmatically query several types of chain state: storage items through api. query, node and chain information through api. rpc, and runtime constants through api. consts. Fourth, you'll learn how the A P I returns data: its Codec wrappers and Option types. You will practice converting Codec results into human-readable or numeric JavaScript values with methods like toHuman, toNumber, and toHex, and you will practice checking Option values with isSome before unwrap. Each objective is paired with a concrete task and competency milestone so you can verify you have mastered the skill. Together these outcomes let you move from manual exploration to automated, testable code that your dApp or backend can depend on.

screens.title: Scaffold a Node.js project and install @polkadot/api
screens.subtitle: Create a project directory and add the core package needed to interact with Substrate

narration.text: The first practical step is scaffolding a minimal Node. js project and installing the Polkadot-JS A P I package. Start by creating a folder, initializing npm, and installing @polkadot/api. This gives you the main classes used throughout the chapter. When you run npm init -y you get a package manifest that lets you manage dependencies and scripts. Installing @polkadot/api with npm install @polkadot/api pulls the library into node_modules so you can require or import ApiPromise and WsProvider. A common novice mistake is running these commands without a network connection or inside the wrong directory; always confirm you are in your project folder. If you plan to use TypeScript, initialize tsconfig and install types, but the core concepts are identical. The important idea is that the library is a dependency of your project, not a global tool. After installation, create a simple file such as index. js and add a placeholder console log to verify node executes the file. This initial step seems trivial, but it's essential: without the package installed and a valid package. json, scripts and tooling will fail. Have your local Substrate dev node ready for the next step so you can immediately test a connection.

screens.title: Connect with WsProvider and ApiPromise
screens.subtitle: Create a provider, await ApiPromise.create, and confirm the node connection

narration.text: Connecting to a Substrate node programmatically is the essential runtime step. The two classes you use are WsProvider, which opens a WebSocket URL, and ApiPromise, which wraps the connection lifecycle in a promise-based A P I. The canonical pattern is to construct a provider with the node endpoint, then await ApiPromise. create with that provider. If you do not await ApiPromise. create and immediately access api fields, you'll see errors because the internal registry and metadata may not be initialized. In the provided example the default dev node URL is ws://127.0.0.1:9944. After the api is ready, you can inspect properties such as genesisHash and runtimeVersion. Always call api. disconnect when your script completes to gracefully close the WebSocket. A practical run: create index. js with the example, start your local Substrate dev node, and run node index. js. If you see connection timeouts check the URL prefix and port: a missing ws:// or wrong port is the most common cause. This walkthrough shows a minimal connection and forms the foundation for all queries that follow. Connect with WsProvider and ApiPromise means always await apipromise.create({ provider }) so the api is fully initialized before you use it; otherwise operations will fail.. In practical terms, create a provider, await apipromise.create, and confirm the node connection. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Await the API
keyIdea.text: Always await ApiPromise.create({ provider }) so the API is fully initialized before you use it; otherwise operations will fail.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.2 › Connection

Connection code walk-through

This script shows the minimal lifecycle: provider, create, use, disconnect. Note the await which ensures readiness.
// index.js
const { ApiPromise, WsProvider } = require('@polkadot/api');

async function main () {
  const provider = new WsProvider('ws://127.0.0.1:9944');
  const api = await ApiPromise.create({ provider });

  console.log(`Connected to chain: ${api.genesisHash.toHex()}`);
  console.log(`Node name: ${api.runtimeVersion.specName.toString()}`);
  console.log(`Node version: ${api.runtimeVersion.implVersion.toNumber()}`);

  await api.disconnect();
}

main().catch(console.error);
Common mistakes
  • Forgetting await on ApiPromise.create leads to uninitialized metadata errors.
  • Incorrect WebSocket URL or missing ws:// prefix causes timeouts.
  • Not disconnecting leaves open sockets during repeated runs.
Check
Ensure your node is running, then run node index.js and expect a chain genesis hash and node version in the console.

screens.title: Understanding the api object structure
screens.subtitle: api.query, api.rpc, api.consts and where to find functionality

narration.text: Once you have a connected ApiPromise instance, the api object exposes distinct areas of functionality that map directly to the node and runtime. api. query gives you access to runtime storage items and mirrors the pallet structure you saw in the Apps UI. Use it to read accounts, balances, or any pallet storage. api. rpc exposes node RPC methods that return node and blockchain data such as the chain name or raw blocks. api. consts provides runtime constants defined by pallets — for example the existential deposit from the Balances pallet. There are also api. tx for submitting transactions and api. events for decoding emitted events. Recognizing which sub-object to use is practical: use api. query for typed runtime storage, api. consts for compile-time constants, and api. rpc for lower-level node queries. A frequent confusion is expecting a constant to appear in api. query; if the value is a constant in the runtime, it will reside under api. consts. Understanding this separation prevents unnecessary lookups and simplifies your scripts. Think of the api as a toolbox where each drawer corresponds to a class of operation.

keyIdea.title: API namespaces
keyIdea.text: api.query for storage, api.rpc for node RPCs, api.consts for runtime constants — use the correct namespace to find what you need quickly.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.2 › API Structure

api namespaces explained

This panel defines each major api sub-object with a short example to anchor understanding. Knowing where to look reduces trial-and-error and helps you write concise queries.
api.query
Typed access to runtime storage. Example: api.query.system.account(address) returns the account info Codec.
api.rpc
Node-level JSON-RPC calls such as api.rpc.system.chain() and api.rpc.chain.getBlockHash().
api.consts
Runtime constants defined by pallets like balances.existentialDeposit.
api.tx & api.events
api.tx helps construct and send extrinsics; api.events decodes events from blocks.
Misconception
Runtime constants are not stored under api.query. If you cannot find a value in api.query, check api.consts.
Check your understanding

Ask: Is this data a storage item, a constant, or a node-level property? That determines the api path you use.

screens.title: Query an account balance and decode the result
screens.subtitle: Use api.query.system.account and convert Codec types to readable values

narration.text: A typical first query is inspecting an account's free balance and nonce. The A P I call api. query. system. account returns an AccountInfo Codec object with fields such as nonce and data. The data field contains the balance object, and to extract usable JavaScript values you must call conversion methods. Common conversions are toNumber for numeric types, toHuman for readable formatting with token units, and toHex for raw hex. In the example we query Alice's well-known development address and destructure the result to extract nonce and balance. Then we log the nonce as a number and the free balance in human form. This illustrates how Codec wraps typed runtime values so you preserve type safety and can still render clear user-facing strings. A frequent error is treating the returned value as a plain number; it's a Codec with methods. Always inspect the shape in the console using toHuman during development so you know which field to use in your application. This practice avoids surprises when data structures differ between runtimes. Query an account balance and decode the result means api.query.system.account returns a codec; use .tonumber(), .tohuman(), or .tohex() to convert fields for display or calculation.. In practical terms, use api.query.system.account and convert codec types to readable values. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.2 › Account Query

Querying an account

Use the system.account storage entry to get nonce and balance. Convert the returned Codec fields to JavaScript-friendly values before using them in UI or calculations.
// inside an async context
const ALICE = '5GrwvaEF5zXb26Fz9rcQpDWS57CtERHpNehXCPcNoHGKutQY';
const { nonce, data: balance } = await api.query.system.account(ALICE);
console.log(`Alice's nonce: ${nonce.toNumber()}, Balance: ${balance.free.toHuman()} ${api.registry.chainTokens[0]}`);
Use toNumber for counters and toHuman for readable token amounts.
Mistake to avoid
Treating the returned value as a raw number will lead to runtime errors. Always use conversion helpers on Codec objects.
Example output
Alice's nonce: 0, Balance: 1000 Unit

screens.title: Handle Option<T> and optional storage values safely
screens.subtitle: Check isSome before unwrap when a storage item may be absent

narration.text: Substrate storage can contain optional values, which the Polkadot-JS A P I represents as Option types. When you query a storage item that might not be set, such as a template pallet's Something value, the A P I returns an Option wrapper. Before you call unwrap to access the inner value, call isSome to check that the value exists. Failing to do so throws an error at runtime. The pattern is straightforward: await the query, test option. isSome, then option. unwrap and apply conversion methods like toNumber. This pattern is especially common with custom pallets and maps. Another helpful practice during development is to log option. toHuman to inspect the shape in the console; that helps you learn whether the value is None or Some. Remember that presence checks and graceful fallbacks in your code make your application robust across chain states. If you plan to display the value in a UI, show an explicit placeholder when the Option is None, avoiding confusing or empty displays for your users. Handle Option<T> and optional storage values safely means always check option.issome before calling unwrap() to avoid runtime errors when storage entries are absent.. In practical terms, check issome before unwrap when a storage item may be absent. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Option handling
keyIdea.text: Always check option.isSome before calling unwrap() to avoid runtime errors when storage entries are absent.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.2 › Option Types

Option<T> handling

When querying custom pallet storage, treat results as Option wrappers. Use isSome to guard unwrap. This prevents uncaught exceptions.
// example after api is ready
const somethingValue = await api.query.templateModule.something();
if (somethingValue.isSome) {
  console.log(`TemplateModule.Something: ${somethingValue.unwrap().toNumber()}`);
} else {
  console.log('TemplateModule.Something is not set.');
}
Developer tip
During debugging, call toHuman() on the Option to reveal its structure; it will show None or Some(value) and help confirm your unwrap logic.
Why it matters

Graceful handling avoids crashes and gives a clearer user experience when runtime state is absent.

screens.title: Use api.rpc and api.consts for node and constant data
screens.subtitle: When to use RPC calls and where runtime constants live

narration.text: The api. rpc and api. consts surfaces serve distinct roles. Use api. rpc for information provided by the node's JSON-RPC layer, such as the chain name, node name, or raw block and metadata retrieval. These calls are appropriate when you need node-level context or access to mechanics like block hash retrieval. In contrast, api. consts contains runtime constants baked into the runtime, like existentialDeposit or block weights. Constants are not queried from storage but read directly from the runtime metadata and are ideal for configuration values you rely on in code. A short code sample demonstrates fetching chain, node name, and version in parallel with Promise. all to reduce round trips. For constants, simply read api. consts. balances. existentialDeposit and convert it with toHuman for display. Being explicit about why you use rpc versus consts avoids confusing runtime values with transient storage items and keeps your code both faster and more semantically correct. Use api.rpc and api.consts for node and constant data means use api.rpc for node info and raw blockchain data; use api.consts for runtime constants defined by pallets.. In practical terms, when to use rpc calls and where runtime constants live. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: RPC vs constants
keyIdea.text: Use api.rpc for node info and raw blockchain data; use api.consts for runtime constants defined by pallets.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.2 › RPC & Consts

Node RPC and runtime constants

// parallel fetch example
const [chain, nodeName, nodeVersion] = await Promise.all([
  api.rpc.system.chain(),
  api.rpc.system.name(),
  api.rpc.system.version()
]);
console.log(`Connected to chain ${chain} using ${nodeName} v${nodeVersion}`);

// read a constant
const existentialDeposit = api.consts.balances.existentialDeposit;
console.log(`Existential Deposit: ${existentialDeposit.toHuman()} units`);
Practical note
Reading constants is cheap and stable. Use rpc for dynamic node or chain metadata and when you need raw block-level access.
Checking both areas helps you understand which values are compile-time constants versus runtime storage or node-level properties.

screens.title: Query diverse chain state in a single script
screens.subtitle: Write query.js to fetch block number, existential deposit, total issuance, validators or events, and metadata

narration.text: This hands-on exercise brings the earlier pieces together into a single script you can run locally. Create query. js, connect to the node, and perform a set of representative queries: the current block number from system. number, a runtime constant like ExistentialDeposit, total token issuance from balances. totalIssuance, and either the current validator set or recent system events depending on available pallets. Also fetch the chain metadata via api. rpc. state. getMetadata and log a concise part, such as the metadata version, to avoid printing huge objects. The exercise demonstrates parallel and sequential queries and how to handle optional query paths — for example, check api. query. session. validators exists before calling it, otherwise fall back to system events. The provided script includes safety checks and console logs to help you inspect results. Running this script while your dev node is active gives immediate feedback about chain state and helps you practice reading Codec outputs and formatting results for display or further processing. keyIdea.title: Comprehensive query script
keyIdea.text: A single query.js demonstrates common reads: block number, constants, issuance, validators or events, and metadata with safe checks and concise logs.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.2 › Query Exercise

Query.js example

// query.js
const { ApiPromise, WsProvider } = require('@polkadot/api');

async function main () {
  const provider = new WsProvider('ws://127.0.0.1:9944');
  const api = await ApiPromise.create({ provider });

  console.log('--- Chain Information ---');
  const chain = await api.rpc.system.chain();
  console.log(`Connected to chain: ${chain}`);

  console.log('
--- Querying State ---');
  const blockNumber = await api.query.system.number();
  console.log(`Current block number: ${blockNumber.toNumber()}`);

  const existentialDeposit = api.consts.balances.existentialDeposit;
  console.log(`Existential Deposit: ${existentialDeposit.toHuman()} units`);

  const totalIssuance = await api.query.balances.totalIssuance();
  console.log(`Total Issuance: ${totalIssuance.toHuman()} units`);

  await api.disconnect();
}

main().catch(console.error);
Run this script with node query.js while your Substrate dev node is running. Expect numeric conversions for block number and human-readable strings for token amounts.
Tip
If a session pallet is not present, check api.query.system.events() as a fallback to inspect recent events.

screens.title: Common pitfalls and debugging strategies
screens.subtitle: Missing await, incorrect WsProvider URL, Option unwrap errors, and verbose metadata

narration.text: When things go wrong, knowing common failure modes saves time. First, forgetting to await ApiPromise. create is the most frequent cause of 'undefined' or metadata errors; always await the promise before using api fields. Second, an incorrect WebSocket URL or missing ws:// prefix produces connection timeouts; check the port and ensure your node is listening. Third, attempting to unwrap an Option without checking isSome will throw. Guard all optional reads to avoid crashes. Fourth, chain metadata is large; logging the entire object produces overwhelming console output. Instead, log metadata. version or other small subsets during development. For connection issues, increase logging detail or run the node with verbose output to see handshake failures. When a query returns unexpected types, use toHuman to reveal the exact structure. Finally, always call api. disconnect in a finally block or after a successful run to close sockets. These debugging habits make your scripts robust and keep your development loop fast and predictable. Common pitfalls and debugging strategies means validate awaits, check websocket endpoints, guard option unwraps, and avoid logging entire large metadata objects to keep debugging effective.. In practical terms, missing await, incorrect wsprovider url, option unwrap errors, and verbose metadata. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.text: Validate awaits, check WebSocket endpoints, guard Option unwraps, and avoid logging entire large metadata objects to keep debugging effective.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.2 › Debugging

Pitfalls and fixes

Quick reference of common errors and how to resolve them with minimal friction.
  • Missing await on ApiPromise.create → await the call.
  • Wrong ws:// URL → verify host and port and include ws:// prefix.
  • Option unwrap without isSome → check isSome first.
  • Logging full metadata → log metadata.version instead.
Debug checklist
Ensure node is running, confirm network reachability, inspect errors from api.create, and use toHuman to inspect Codec shapes during development.
Recovery
Wrap connection code in try/catch and always call api.disconnect in a finally block to keep sockets clean across runs.

screens.title: Using the API in a dApp or backend
screens.subtitle: Architectural considerations for where and how to use Polkadot-JS API in your system

narration.text: When you move from scripts to a dApp or backend service, consider where the A P I instance lives and how it's reused. ApiPromise objects maintain metadata and type registries, so creating an ApiPromise for every request is inefficient. Instead, create a shared ApiPromise instance that your application reuses for the process lifetime. On the server side, manage provider reconnection logic and handle transient network errors. For frontends, prefer lightweight JSON APIs that proxy chain reads to avoid exposing node endpoints directly; this also centralizes conversion logic for Codec types. When building reactive UIs, use subscriptions sparingly — api. query supports subscription callbacks but they keep sockets open and produce continual updates. Use polling or targeted subscriptions depending on your scale. Finally, document which api namespaces your service reads and which extrinsics it submits. This clarity helps teams reason about performance, caching, and security boundaries when integrating Polkadot-JS A P I into production systems. Using the API in a dApp or backend means reuse a single apipromise per process, centralize conversions, and choose subscriptions carefully to balance realtime needs and resource usage.. In practical terms, architectural considerations for where and how to use polkadot-js api in your system. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Instance strategy
keyIdea.text: Reuse a single ApiPromise per process, centralize conversions, and choose subscriptions carefully to balance realtime needs and resource usage.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.2 › Architecture

Where the API fits

Reuse ApiPromise instances to avoid reinitializing type registries. For server apps create a long-lived connection and add reconnection logic.
Patterns
  • Shared backend ApiPromise with caching and conversion helpers.
  • Frontend proxies to avoid direct node exposure.
  • Careful subscription use for real-time needs.
Security & scale
Centralizing chain reads lets you enforce rate limits, sanitize outputs, and cache expensive conversions so clients remain fast and secure.
Document which api.* namespaces your service uses so teams can reason about state dependencies and operational requirements.

screens.title: From queries to transactions and events
screens.subtitle: How this chapter prepares you for constructing extrinsics and handling events

narration.text: This chapter's focus on connection and queries prepares you to construct and submit transactions and to decode events in later lessons. With a reliable ApiPromise instance you will later use api. tx to build extrinsics, sign them with keypairs, and submit them via signAndSend or send. You will also use api. events or parse block events after a block is produced to observe state changes triggered by transactions. The conversion and Option handling patterns you've practiced are directly applicable: responses from extrinsic submission and event payloads are returned as Codecs and must be interpreted with the same conversion helpers. Additionally, knowing where constants and queries live helps you validate preconditions before sending transactions, such as checking an account's balance against existentialDeposit before transferring tokens. This chapter therefore establishes the safe coding practices and debugging habits required for writing robust transactions and responding to on-chain events in production code. narration.text: A final set of reminders to keep your development efficient: always await ApiPromise. create to ensure the A P I is ready; inspect returned values with conversion helpers instead of assuming plain JavaScript types; and guard Option unwraps with isSome.
